text: An older adult with type 2 diabetes presents with profound dehydration, confusion, plasma glucose of 42 mmol/L, high serum osmolality, minimal ketones, and potassium of 3.0 mmol/L. Intravenous isotonic fluid has been started. What is the most appropriate next step before starting insulin?

No testing until symptoms have lasted six weeks
rationale: In high or likely pre-test probability, duplex ultrasound should be performed rather than relying on D-dimer alone. A negative D-dimer is not the appropriate sole exclusion strategy in a high-probability presentation.

text: Six days after knee replacement, a patient has new unilateral calf swelling and tenderness. Clinical suspicion for DVT is high. Compression ultrasound is not available until the next day, there is no active bleeding, and the surgical team identifies no contraindication to anticoagulation. What is the most appropriate plan?
options: Start anticoagulant treatment while arranging imaging as soon as possible
Wait without treatment for one month
Give warfarin alone and never obtain imaging
Start an antibiotic and cancel vascular assessment
rationale: When compression ultrasound is not rapidly available, Thrombosis Canada advises starting anticoagulation for moderate-to-high clinical suspicion when bleeding risk is not high, while arranging imaging as soon as possible. Anticoagulant choice and postoperative bleeding assessment remain patient-specific.

text: A 57-year-old postmenopausal patient had a low-trauma wrist fracture that was assessed as osteoporosis-related. What is the most appropriate next preventive assessment?
options: Arrange bone mineral density testing and calculate 10-year fracture risk using Canada-specific FRAX with BMD when available
Wait until age 70 before considering any bone-health assessment
Start indefinite medication without assessing fracture risk or bone density
Recommend calcium alone and do not assess fracture risk
Order a screening mammogram as the osteoporosis investigation
rationale: Osteoporosis Canada suggests BMD testing for postmenopausal people aged 50 to 64 with a previous osteoporosis-related fracture. The preferred tool for estimating 10-year fracture risk is Canada-specific FRAX with BMD, with CAROC as an alternative. This assessment guides the treatment decision rather than assuming every fracture has the same threshold.

text: A 61-year-old postmenopausal patient meets the Health Canada calcium recommended daily allowance through food. They ask whether to add a large daily calcium supplement solely for fracture prevention. What is the best advice?
options: Do not add routine extra calcium solely to exceed the recommended daily allowance when dietary intake is already sufficient
Add calcium indefinitely regardless of total dietary intake
Stop all dietary calcium because supplements are preferred
Use calcium as a replacement for fracture-risk assessment
Avoid physical activity because it increases fracture risk
rationale: Osteoporosis Canada suggests no extra calcium supplementation for people who already meet the Health Canada recommended daily allowance through diet. Bone health also includes fall prevention, exercise, vitamin D according to guidance and individualized fracture-risk assessment; supplements are not a substitute for those decisions.

text: A 23-year-old with type 1 diabetes has abdominal pain, vomiting, deep rapid breathing, glucose of 24 mmol/L, positive blood ketones, and metabolic acidosis. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Simple isolated hyperglycemia with no emergency
rationale: DKA and HHS are both hyperglycemic emergencies. In this presentation, ketones and metabolic acidosis in a person with insulin deficiency support DKA. The initial plan addresses volume depletion, electrolytes, insulin sequence, monitoring, and the precipitating cause.

text: An older adult with type 2 diabetes is profoundly dehydrated and confused. Glucose is 43 mmol/L, serum osmolality is high, and ketones are minimal with no substantial acidosis. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Diabetic ketoacidosis as defined by marked ketoacidosis
rationale: HHS is characterized by marked hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, and severe fluid depletion, usually with absent or limited ketoacidosis. It overlaps with DKA in electrolyte and volume losses, so both require careful monitored emergency management.

text: A patient with DKA has a potassium concentration of 2.9 mmol/L after initial assessment. Which change to the usual insulin sequence is most important?
options: Replace potassium and withhold insulin until potassium is safely corrected
Start insulin immediately and delay potassium replacement
Give bicarbonate only and ignore potassium
Use oral carbohydrate as the only treatment
Discharge because the glucose concentration will lower with fasting
rationale: Insulin shifts potassium into cells. With marked hypokalemia, starting insulin first can precipitate dangerous arrhythmia and muscle weakness. Potassium repletion and close monitoring must come before insulin when potassium is severely low.

text: A patient with DKA has a pH of 7.16 after initial fluids. Which statement about bicarbonate therapy is most accurate?
options: Routine bicarbonate is not indicated; it may be considered only for extreme acidosis such as pH 7.0 or lower
Bicarbonate should be given to every patient with DKA
Bicarbonate replaces fluid resuscitation and insulin
Bicarbonate is required whenever glucose exceeds 14 mmol/L
Bicarbonate should be given before any electrolyte measurement
rationale: Diabetes Canada notes that bicarbonate therapy may be considered only for extreme acidosis at pH 7.0 or lower. Standard DKA management focuses on fluid and electrolyte replacement, insulin once safe, frequent reassessment, and treatment of the trigger.

text: A critically ill adult with diabetes is admitted to the intensive care unit. Which inpatient blood-glucose target is recommended by Diabetes Canada when it can be achieved safely?
options: Maintain blood glucose between 6.0 and 10.0 mmol/L
Use no target because glucose does not affect critical illness
Aim for zero glucose variability by withholding all insulin
rationale: For critically ill hospitalized people with diabetes, Diabetes Canada recommends maintaining blood glucose between 6.0 and 10.0 mmol/L. Avoiding hypoglycemia remains essential, so targets must be achieved with safe monitoring and treatment.

text: A noncritically ill hospital patient with diabetes is eating regular meals and has no recurrent hypoglycemia. Which target framework is most appropriate when safely achievable?
options: Preprandial glucose 5.0 to 8.0 mmol/L with random glucose below 10.0 mmol/L
Glucose must be below 2.0 mmol/L before each meal
Allow random glucose above 30 mmol/L to avoid all hypoglycemia
Use no glucose monitoring outside intensive care
Give insulin only after a diabetic emergency occurs
rationale: For most noncritically ill hospitalized people with diabetes, Diabetes Canada recommends preprandial values of 5.0 to 8.0 mmol/L and random values below 10.0 mmol/L when these targets can be achieved safely.

text: A 34-year-old has brief pleuritic chest pain. The clinician judges pulmonary embolism probability to be low, and all eight Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria (PERC) are negative. Vital signs are normal. What is the best next step?
rationale: In a patient with low empirical pretest probability and all PERC items negative, PE can be excluded without D-dimer or imaging.

sub: Negative D-dimer in suspected pulmonary embolism
text: A hemodynamically stable 46-year-old has an unlikely clinical pretest probability of PE. A highly sensitive D-dimer is negative. What is the best next step?
options: Repeat D-dimer daily for one week
rationale: A negative highly sensitive D-dimer excludes PE in a patient with low, moderate, or unlikely pretest probability; imaging is unnecessary.

text: A 62-year-old with active cancer has sudden dyspnea, tachycardia, hemoptysis, and unilateral leg swelling. PE is clinically likely. The patient is stable and CT contrast is not contraindicated. Which diagnostic test is most appropriate next?
rationale: A likely or high pretest probability should proceed directly to diagnostic imaging. D-dimer is not the appropriate rule-out test in this group.

text: A 72-year-old has a non-high pretest probability of PE. The D-dimer is 650 micrograms/L FEU. The laboratory uses an age-adjusted threshold for patients 50 years or older. What is the best interpretation?
options: The result is positive because every adult cutoff is 500
The result is negative because the age-adjusted cutoff is 720
The result is uninterpretable after age 70
rationale: For patients 50 years or older, an age-adjusted threshold of age multiplied by 10 micrograms/L FEU may be used. At age 72, 650 is below 720 and is negative in a non-high PTP pathway.

sub: Empiric anticoagulation while awaiting PE imaging
text: A stable patient has a likely PE, no major bleeding risk, and no contraindication to anticoagulation. CT pulmonary angiography will be delayed for six hours. What is the best management while awaiting imaging?
rationale: When diagnostic testing will be delayed more than about four hours in a patient with moderate/high or likely probability and low bleeding risk, start a rapidly acting anticoagulant while testing is arranged.

sub: Outpatient treatment of low-risk pulmonary embolism
text: A stable patient has a confirmed PE, very low PESI risk, no oxygen requirement, no need for parenteral analgesia, no severe renal dysfunction or high bleeding risk, and reliable home support. What is the best disposition?
options: Consider outpatient treatment or early discharge with reliable follow-up
Admit every patient with PE to intensive care
Insert an IVC filter before outpatient care
rationale: Carefully selected low-risk patients can be considered for outpatient management or early discharge when clinical, bleeding, renal, social, and follow-up criteria are favorable.

text: A patient with confirmed PE is confused, cool, and diaphoretic with a blood pressure of 80/50 mm Hg despite initial resuscitation. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Urgently assess for reperfusion therapy such as systemic thrombolysis
rationale: Hemodynamic instability defines high-risk PE. Alongside resuscitation and anticoagulation when appropriate, urgent reperfusion assessment is required; systemic thrombolysis is the usual immediate option when not contraindicated.

text: A patient has a newly confirmed symptomatic proximal lower-extremity DVT and no contraindication to anticoagulation. What is the minimum standard treatment duration?
rationale: A confirmed proximal DVT requires therapeutic anticoagulation for at least three months. Whether therapy continues longer depends on provoking factors, recurrence risk, bleeding risk, and preferences.

text: A stable nonpregnant adult with a new DVT wants an oral regimen that can begin immediately without a preceding course of LMWH. Renal and hepatic function are adequate. Which option fits?
options: Dabigatran alone from the first dose
Edoxaban alone from the first dose
rationale: Apixaban and rivaroxaban can be used as single-drug oral regimens with their initial higher-dose phases. Dabigatran and edoxaban require initial parenteral anticoagulation.

text: A patient with acute PE will receive dabigatran for ongoing treatment. What must occur before dabigatran is started?
options: Five to ten days of therapeutic parenteral anticoagulation
Placement of a vena cava filter
rationale: Dabigatran and edoxaban require five to ten days of initial therapeutic LMWH or another suitable parenteral anticoagulant before the oral agent begins.

text: An ambulatory patient has a small isolated distal calf DVT, mild symptoms, low risk of extension, high bleeding risk, and reliable follow-up. What is the best initial strategy?
options: Serial compression ultrasound about weekly for two weeks
rationale: Selected low-risk isolated distal DVT can be monitored with serial ultrasound, approximately weekly for two weeks, instead of immediate anticoagulation. Extension or worsening changes management.

text: A patient has sudden massive leg swelling, severe pain, cyanosis, and a weak distal pulse from extensive iliofemoral DVT. What is the best next step?
options: Urgent specialist assessment for invasive clot-removal or reperfusion plus anticoagulation
rationale: Phlegmasia cerulea dolens is limb threatening. It requires immediate anticoagulation and urgent vascular or interventional assessment for thrombus-removal strategies.

text: A patient has an acute proximal DVT and ongoing intracranial bleeding that makes therapeutic anticoagulation temporarily contraindicated. Which intervention may be appropriate?
options: A retrievable inferior vena cava filter
Permanent filter for every future episode
rationale: A retrievable IVC filter may be considered for recent acute proximal DVT or PE when anticoagulation is contraindicated. It does not treat the existing clot and should be temporary whenever possible.

sub: Removal of a retrievable IVC filter
text: A retrievable IVC filter was placed for acute PE during active gastrointestinal bleeding. The bleeding is controlled and therapeutic anticoagulation has begun. What is the best next step regarding the filter?
options: Plan prompt retrieval and document follow-up
Stop anticoagulation because the filter replaces it
Remove it only if another PE occurs
rationale: Once anticoagulation can be given safely, a retrievable filter should be removed as soon as practical. A retrieval plan and responsible follow-up should be documented.

sub: Duration after major transient provoking factor
text: A patient develops proximal DVT two weeks after major surgery. Recovery is complete, mobility is normal, and no persistent risk factor remains. After three months of uneventful anticoagulation, what is generally recommended?
options: Stop anticoagulation after the three-month treatment course
Order residual-vein ultrasound to mandate lifelong treatment
rationale: VTE provoked by a resolved major transient factor has a low recurrence risk. Three months of anticoagulation is generally sufficient when the provoking factor has resolved.

text: A patient completes six months of anticoagulation after a first unprovoked proximal DVT. Bleeding risk is low. What is the best approach to deciding whether to continue?
options: Use residual clot on ultrasound as the only decision
Balance recurrence and bleeding risks with patient preferences, and reassess at least annually if extended
Replace anticoagulation with an IVC filter
rationale: After the initial treatment of unprovoked proximal DVT or PE, extended therapy is an individualized shared decision. If continued, the indication and bleeding risk should be reviewed periodically, at least annually.
